N1.1.label: What AI does today in cyber
N1.1.definition: Describe what AI and agents already do well in one's own domain and the neighbouring ones: triage and enrichment, log and code analysis, drafting and summarising, policy mapping, test generation

N1.2.label: What is emerging
N1.2.definition: Describe what is emerging in AI for cyber, beyond what is in production today

N1.3.label: How one's own work changes
N1.3.definition: Name two or three ways one's own work could change. The purpose is to open the mind to a new way of working, not to teach a tool

N2.1.label: Models
N2.1.definition: Different providers make different models, varying in capability, cost, speed and how much they reason; some are open source and can be hosted by the bank; work is measured in tokens

N2.2.label: Modalities
N2.2.definition: AI handles text, code, images, voice, documents and screens, and can act across them

N2.3.label: Ways of using AI
N2.3.definition: Four patterns: assistant (chat), agent (acts, uses tools, loops until done), teams of agents, and humans and agents working in a shared space

N2.4.label: Anatomy of an agent
N2.4.definition: An agent is a model wrapped in a harness: instructions, memory, tools and a loop; the harness is what people configure

N2.5.label: Connecting and extending
N2.5.definition: Three ways to extend AI: connectors to tools and data (MCP), reusable playbooks (Skills), and APIs for building

N2.6.label: Safety components
N2.6.definition: Every safe deployment has an identity and permissions for the agent, a sandbox it runs in, an authorisation layer that decides what it may do, guardrails on input and output, logs of what it did, and a stop button

N2.7.label: Where it runs
N2.7.definition: The bank's approved platforms versus public tools, and what leaves the bank with each

N3.1.label: Hallucination
N3.1.definition: Hallucination and confident wrong answers: explain them and recognise them in one's own tools

N3.2.label: Sycophancy
N3.2.definition: The model agreeing with the user; recognising it in one's own tools

N3.3.label: Context loss
N3.3.definition: Loss of context in long sessions

N3.4.label: Non-determinism
N3.4.definition: Non-deterministic output: the same input can give different answers

N3.5.label: Prompt injection
N3.5.definition: Prompt injection as a behaviour of the model: content it reads can steer it

N3.6.label: Automation bias
N3.6.definition: Automation bias: the human tendency to over-trust the machine

N3.7.label: Counter-habits
N3.7.definition: The habits that counter these failures: check against sources, record one's own view before reading the AI's, sample rather than trust

N4.1.definition: Data leaving the bank through public tools

N7.1.definition: Scope the task, set boundaries and permissions for the action classes one is signed off on, and check the agent's permissions before handing over

N7.2.label: Monitor
N7.2.definition: Read the agent's trace (plan, tool calls, result), know which permissions it holds and what it has changed, find its logs, notice drift and approval overload

N7.3.label: Verify
N7.3.definition: Sample outputs, trace the evidence, catch planted errors at the target rate

N7.4.label: Intervene
N7.4.definition: Stop, override, roll back and take over mid-task, including when the agent is compromised; keep working when agents are down

N7.5.label: Account
N7.5.definition: Sign off with a record an auditor can follow, own the outcome, feed corrections back

N8.2.label: Maintaining Skills
N8.2.definition: Keeping Skills focused (one task each), reviewing them monthly and retesting them when models or tools change

N8.3.label: Shared library

N8.4.label: Using connectors safely

N8.5.label: Vetting before installing

R1.1.1.label: Agent incident playbooks
R1.1.1.definition: Writing incident playbooks for three agent scenarios: the agent is wrong (it acted on a false conclusion, closed real alerts, changed the wrong thing); the agent is stopped (its identity expired, the provider is down, it ran out of compute) and its work must continue by hand; the agent is compromised (an attacker steered it through content it read). Plans name who can stop the agent (NCSC)

R1.1.2.label: Ways to stop an agent
R1.1.2.definition: The ways to stop an agent and when to use each: revoke its identity or session token so it can no longer call any tool; disable only the tools or connectors it misuses while the rest keeps running; put it in observe-only mode, where it may analyse and recommend but is barred from acting; roll back what it changed using its action log

R1.1.3.label: Investigating a compromised agent
R1.1.3.definition: Where the attack comes from: content the agent reads (logs, alerts, tickets, documents, emails, web pages) can carry instructions aimed at it, so the investigator looks for injection in those sources and cuts any that is poisoned. What the agent did: knowing, for each of the bank's agents, which records exist that the agent cannot write to and how to pull them fast (the platform's audit log of tool calls with arguments and times, gateway and network logs, logs of the systems it touched), then building the timeline from them, because a compromised agent's own summary can omit or misstate what it did

R1.1.4.label: Cleaning up
R1.1.4.definition: Cleaning up after a manipulated agent: finding the injected content it acted on and removing it from the sources the agent reads; clearing anything it stored in its memory as a result; re-running the same injection against the agent before putting it back in service

R1.1.5.label: Operating without the agent
R1.1.5.definition: The manual fallback for what the agent handled (triage queue, enrichment, first response), the staffing to sustain it for days, and the regular drill that proves it still works

R1.1.6.label: Reporting
R1.1.6.definition: What regulators expect in an incident report when an agent caused or worsened the incident (DORA, HKMA, MAS), and which evidence to preserve for it

R1.2.1.label: Recording the AI step
R1.2.1.definition: Recording any AI step applied to evidence so it can be repeated and defended: the tool, model and version, the exact prompt and settings, the output, and who verified it. The original artefact stays the evidence; AI output is a derived analysis, never a substitute

R1.2.2.label: Forensic readiness for agents
R1.2.2.definition: Defining what every agent must log (prompt and response, each tool call with its arguments, data retrieved, memory writes, approvals given), stored where the agent cannot alter it, time-synchronised and integrity-protected, retained long enough for an investigation (vendors default to 7 to 30 days), and tested by reconstructing a past incident from it

R1.2.3.label: Investigating an agent as suspect
R1.2.3.definition: Rebuilding the agent's actions from its traces, finding the input that steered it, and attributing each action to the human it acted for or to the attacker

R3.1.1.label: AI attack classes
R3.1.1.definition: Direct prompt injection; indirect injection through content the agent reads (documents, web pages, tool results, emails); jailbreaks and guardrail evasion; data exfiltration through the agent's own tools; making the agent exceed its intended authority; tool poisoning (a malicious tool description) and rug pulls (a tool that changes after it was approved)

R3.1.2.label: Published methods
R3.1.2.definition: The OWASP GenAI Red Teaming Guide, the Cloud Security Alliance's Agentic AI Red Teaming Guide (12 categories) and MITRE ATLAS techniques

R3.1.3.label: Attacks across agents
R3.1.3.definition: Compromising one agent to steer others, injecting into an orchestrator's plan, tampering with messages between agents

R3.1.4.label: Attacks on model and platform
R3.1.4.definition: Extracting the model or its instructions, poisoning the agent's memory, escaping the sandbox, timing side channels

R3.1.5.label: Automated red-team programme
R3.1.5.definition: Building and running automated red-team harnesses (PyRIT-class tooling) and a continuous programme that re-tests every agent when its model, tools or prompts change

R3.2.1.label: Containment before a run
R3.2.1.definition: A network segment from which the agent can reach only in-scope targets; egress allow-lists verified by test, not assumed; a fresh sandbox per run; credentials scoped to the engagement and expiring with it

R3.2.2.label: Monitoring during a run
R3.2.2.definition: Watching the agent's actions out of band (not its reports); a named person with the authority and the means to kill the run within minutes; the triggers for doing so (an action outside scope, contact with a third party, a credential used elsewhere)

R3.2.3.label: Escape patterns
R3.2.3.definition: The escape patterns seen in practice: attacking something else when the assigned target proves impossible, reading an ambiguous message as approval, creating accounts or identities, carrying on after the window closes, contacting real people

R3.2.4.label: Trajectory-level validation
R3.2.4.definition: Validating findings from the transcript, not the summary: check that the evidence the agent cites exists (a 'successful login' that was a redirect, credentials that do not work), reproduce the exploit by hand before reporting, and treat the agent's self-assessment as untrusted

R3.2.5.label: Collateral findings
R3.2.5.definition: A disclosure lane for what to do when the agent finds something outside the engagement

R4.1.1.label: Discovery
R4.1.1.definition: Finding every MCP server and agent connector in the estate, including those developers run on their own workstations, by searching configuration files and by recognising the MCP protocol in network traffic

R4.1.2.label: Inventory
R4.1.2.definition: For each agent and tool server: its owner, version, the tools it exposes, the permissions it holds, the systems it reaches, and the guardrails around it

R4.1.3.label: Content-bound approval
R4.1.3.definition: Approving a tool by the hash of its description and code, and checking each session that it has not been silently redefined since (the rug pull)

R4.1.4.label: Scanning
R4.1.4.definition: Running MCP and Skill scanners in the build pipeline and on a schedule for tool poisoning, instructions hidden in tool descriptions, servers exposed without authentication and credentials stored in plain text

R4.1.5.label: AI bill of materials
R4.1.5.definition: A bill of materials for AI components: which models, tools and Skills a system uses and where each came from

R4.1.6.label: Vetting third parties
R4.1.6.definition: Vetting third-party Skills and connectors before they are allowed in

R4.2.1.label: Why set-up is the skill
R4.2.1.definition: The same model finds under a tenth or over half of the vulnerabilities in a codebase depending on how it is given context and driven, and filters a third or almost all of a static analyser's false positives for the same reason

R4.2.2.label: Giving the model context
R4.2.2.definition: Supplying the functions a target calls, type definitions, the data-flow path to the input and build information, using static and dynamic analysis tools to supply that context automatically

R4.2.3.label: Framework, model and method
R4.2.3.definition: Choosing the agent framework and the model for the task, and driving the model through a structured method rather than letting it explore freely

R4.2.4.label: Confirming before reporting
R4.2.4.definition: A proof of vulnerability (an input or exploit that demonstrates it in a sandbox), the same test against the patched and unpatched versions, and several runs with a majority verdict

R4.2.5.label: Reliability by vulnerability class
R4.2.5.definition: Which classes models find well (memory safety, anything a fuzzer can reach) and which they over-report (documented behaviour reported as a bug, inflated severity, duplicates), and setting thresholds per class

R4.2.6.label: Deduplication and cost
R4.2.6.definition: Removing duplicates (by stack trace or sanitiser signature) and keeping cost under control at scale

R4.2.7.label: Measuring the harness
R4.2.7.definition: Measuring the harness on a corpus of known vulnerabilities before trusting it

R5.1.1.label: Classifying agent actions
R5.1.1.definition: For each action an agent can take in a process (a payment, a data deletion, an email to a client, a firewall change), rating its impact and whether it can be undone, and assigning a tier: autonomous, autonomous with logging, human approval, two-person approval, prohibited

R5.1.2.label: Enforcement outside the model
R5.1.2.definition: An authorisation point between the agent's plan and its execution that checks every action against its tier and the agent's permissions, so the decision never depends on the model obeying its instructions

R5.1.3.label: The stop mechanism
R5.1.3.definition: No standard defines a kill switch, so it is designed as a set of levers (interrupt the task, revoke credentials, cut tool access, quarantine the agent, roll back its changes), each with who may trigger it, how fast it takes effect and how it is tested

R5.1.4.label: The audit trail
R5.1.4.definition: What is recorded (reasoning artefacts, each tool call with its arguments, data accessed, messages between agents, approvals), where (a store the agent cannot write to), for how long, and how each action is tied to the person the agent acted for

R5.1.5.label: The oversight interface
R5.1.5.definition: How an approval request is shown so a person can judge it (what will happen, in plain language, with the risk and the agent's confidence), limiting the volume of requests so approvers do not click through them, and what overseers must be trained on

R5.1.6.label: Reference architectures
R5.1.6.definition: Reference architectures for the bank's agent platforms and how the above is implemented on each

R6.1.1.label: Agent control catalogue
R6.1.1.definition: The control catalogue for agents and how to test each control: a distinct identity and permissions per agent, tool allow-lists, logging that the agent cannot alter, approval gates for high-impact actions, change control on prompts, tools and models

R6.1.2.label: Assuring assurance's own AI
R6.1.2.definition: Documenting, validating and monitoring the AI used to produce assessments and gather evidence

R9.1.1.label: Registering an agent
R9.1.1.definition: Its own identity (never a shared or human credential), a human sponsor recorded in the directory who is accountable for it, a stated purpose and a declared list of what it may do

R9.1.2.label: Delegated authority
R9.1.2.definition: Issuing and reading tokens in which the subject is the person and the actor is the agent (token exchange, on-behalf-of flows), with the person's consent recorded, and what the agent may then do in that person's name

R9.1.3.label: Connector and MCP scopes
R9.1.3.definition: Reading what a scope actually permits in the bank's applications and tool servers, granting the minimum, and reviewing grants

R9.1.4.label: Just-in-time access
R9.1.4.definition: Privilege granted for a task and a time window with no standing privilege, and the conditions that require a human to approve the grant

R9.1.5.label: Short-lived sub-agents
R9.1.5.definition: Identities that exist for seconds, with a time to live and no more rights than the parent

R9.1.6.label: Recertification
R9.1.6.definition: Quarterly for agents and monthly for high-privilege ones, with de-provisioning triggered when the sponsor leaves or the purpose lapses

R9.1.7.label: Revocation drills
R9.1.7.definition: Revoking an agent's identity and its live sessions within minutes, and verifying that it worked

R9.1.8.label: Integration with IGA, PAM, SIEM
R9.1.8.definition: Integrating the agent authorisation point with identity governance, privileged access and the SIEM: registration, scoped issuance, just-in-time grants, recertification and revocation signals flowing between them

R9.1.9.label: Privileged access and break-glass
R9.1.9.definition: Privileged access and break-glass for agents inside the existing privileged-access model

R9.1.10.label: Audit trail and standards
R9.1.10.definition: The audit trail regulators ask for (which agent, on whose behalf, which tools, what data, what reasoning) and the standards still being written (IETF agent identity, OpenID AuthZEN, MCP authorisation), so the design does not lock into one vendor's delegation model
